Mike Rogers clobbered Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate debate on Thursday night in Grand Rapids, and called him out to his face for being a fake doctor. This was the first time a lot of voters heard it said, and it landed hard.

El-Sayed calls himself a doctor and a physician. He has a medical degree from Columbia and a four-week internship at a Manhattan hospital. He doesn’t have a medical license. Read that again. He doesn’t have a medical license, and he still calls himself a doctor. Rogers said it plainly. If a patient walked into El-Sayed’s office and he tried to treat them, he’d go to jail. That’s not a threat. That’s the law.

El-Sayed’s answer was his résumé, his degree, his public-health job, and his claim that Rogers was changing the subject. A degree isn’t a license, and a license is what lets you treat a patient. El-Sayed has been selling himself as a doctor even though he doesn’t have a license to practice as one.

Rogers called the whole pitch a con. He also called out El-Sayed’s dual citizenship, and the way El-Sayed’s own campaign is now contradicting what El-Sayed said about it. El-Sayed said in a 2016 speech that he carries dual citizenship in the United States and Egypt, and his 2014 résumé listed both. His campaign now says he isn’t a dual citizen and never has been. El-Sayed didn’t explain the contradiction on the stage. Instead, he called Rogers weak, cowardly, and a sock puppet for the administration. Rogers’ criticism of El-Sayed is a record a voter can check. El-Sayed’s criticism of Rogers is empty name-calling.

A man like El-Sayed running for the U.S. Senate on health care shouldn’t need a moderator to explain that he can’t legally practice medicine. But that’s precisely what had to happen Thursday night. Michigan voters have now seen the fraud. El-Sayed has been lying his whole campaign about being a doctor, and plenty of Democrats went along with the lie.
